title: The Study Its Own University Asked to Have Retracted
hook: A university audit found a celebrated study had no ethics approval and unverifiable data. Three years later the journal answered with a 78-word correction — and the study kept guiding care.
key_points: Dr. Craig Towers' 2020 study of 230 pregnant patients reported that women could safely detox from opioids, cutting against established medical doctrine.
A University of Tennessee audit found he never obtained institutional review board (IRB) approval and supplied 'inaccurate and/or unverifiable, contradictory source documentation.'
Eight addiction-and-pregnancy specialists questioned the informed consent, the absence of any refusals or dropouts, and the unusually low rate of reported adverse events.
The university's IRB called the findings 'serious noncompliance,' but the correction machinery ran elsewhere — the journal took three years to answer its retraction request.
In 2023 the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology issued a 78-word correction, not a retraction, noting only that the study was retrospective rather than prospective as claimed.
Clinics in Tennessee and Florida had already adopted the detox approach; ProPublica reported the reconstruction, not any regulator.
content_html: Dr. Craig Towers, a high-risk obstetrician who came to the University of Tennessee Medical Center in Knoxville in 2010, published a 2020 study of 230 pregnant patients arguing that women could safely detoxify from opioids during pregnancy — a claim that ran against the prevailing medical doctrine and was widely celebrated. A subsequent university audit, ProPublica reports, found that he had never obtained institutional review board approval, that his source documentation was "inaccurate and/or unverifiable, contradictory," and that he did not hand over the research databases or analysis when asked. Towers, who retired in February 2020 citing health and family reasons, disputes the audit's conclusions.
extra_html: The civics lesson here is about the chain, not the individual. Oversight of published research is split across bodies that each hold one lever: an IRB approves the ethics up front, a university can audit and declare "serious noncompliance," a journal owns the published record, and clinicians decide what to practice. None of them can finish the job alone. Tennessee's audit landed, but the university's retraction request sat with the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology for three years, and the 2023 answer was a 78-word correction noting the study was retrospective rather than prospective — not a retraction. Research-fraud specialist Eugenie Reich told ProPublica the misrepresentation "runs throughout the piece" and was far more serious than the correction acknowledged. Meanwhile clinics in Tennessee and Florida had adopted the approach, and one physician, Dr. Cathleen Suto, reported her own patients were not successful at completing detox. That gap — a finding discredited internally but still standing publicly — is the recurring failure mode of distributed accountability, and it is why investigative journalism so often ends up doing the reconstruction that no single regulator is positioned to do. (U.S. example.)

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Self-Regulation and the Jurisdiction Gap
related.hook: When a private body governs an activity but sits outside every regulator's remit, weak rules stop being a flaw and start being a competitive advantage.

related.title: How Official Statistics Earn Trust
related.hook: A government statistic carries weight only because of the process behind it. When a report skips the usual methodology and review, the number stops being evidence and becomes an argument.

related.title: Three Kinds of Denial That Let Institutions Off the Hook
related.hook: Sociologist Stanley Cohen built a typology to explain how societies wave away state atrocities. It turns out to describe how any institution protects its own — one denial at a time.

flashcards.prompt: What did the University of Tennessee audit find about the study's ethics approval?

choices.text: The researcher never obtained institutional review board (IRB) approval
The IRB approved it but later withdrew consent forms
Approval was granted by a different university's board

flashcards.explanation_html: The audit found no IRB approval at all, alongside "inaccurate and/or unverifiable, contradictory source documentation" — which its IRB classified as serious noncompliance.

flashcards.prompt: Why couldn't the university simply undo the study's influence once its audit was done?
flashcards.back_html: Because the audit and the published record sit in different hands. The university can find noncompliance; only the journal can retract — and it took three years to respond, then issued a 78-word correction.

flashcards.prompt: What does this case illustrate about oversight of published research?

choices.text: Correcting the record depends on several separate bodies acting, and any one of them can stall it
An institutional audit automatically removes a flawed study from the literature
Peer review reliably catches missing ethics approval before publication

flashcards.explanation_html: IRB, university audit, journal, and the clinics using the findings are independent links. Here the audit landed, the journal stalled, and the practice spread regardless.
